title: Digestive Tract & Its Glands
summary: Follow the gut tube and its accessory glands, seeing how each segment's structure matches its job.

lessons.title: Oral Cavity, Teeth & Salivary Glands

levels.kid:
Your mouth is the front door of your gut. It is lined with a soft, tough skin that is many layers thick, like a stack of pancakes. When the top layers rub off from chewing, new ones grow up from below.

Your tongue has tiny bumps called **papillae**. Some of them hold **taste buds**, little clusters of cells that tell you sweet, salty, sour, bitter and savory.

Your teeth are covered in **enamel**, the hardest stuff in your whole body. Under it is **dentin**, and in the middle is the **pulp**, with nerves and blood vessels.

Spit comes from **salivary glands**. They are like bunches of grapes, and each grape squirts saliva into tiny tubes that lead to your mouth.
levels.hs:
The oral cavity begins digestion, and its tissues show how structure fits job.

**Lining.** The mouth is lined by **stratified squamous epithelium**, many cell layers thick, which resists scraping. Where chewing forces are high (gums, hard palate) it is **keratinized**, toughened with the protein keratin. Elsewhere (cheeks, floor of mouth) it is non-keratinized and stays moist.

**Tongue.** The tongue is a mass of **skeletal muscle** running in three directions, which makes it very agile. Its surface has **papillae**:
- **Filiform**: the most numerous, pointed, no taste buds, give grip.
- **Fungiform**: mushroom-shaped, scattered, carry some taste buds.
- **Circumvallate**: about 8-12 large ones in a V at the back, with many taste buds in their trenches.

**Teeth.** A tooth has three hard tissues:
- **Enamel**, about 96% mineral (hydroxyapatite), made by cells called ameloblasts that are lost once the tooth erupts, so enamel cannot regrow.
- **Dentin**, made by **odontoblasts**, which keep working for life.
- **Cementum**, covering the root and anchoring it via the periodontal ligament.

**Salivary glands.** The **parotid**, **submandibular** and **sublingual** glands make about 1 to 1.5 liters of saliva a day. **Serous** cells make watery, enzyme-rich fluid (like amylase, which starts starch digestion); **mucous** cells make thick mucus. Example: the parotid is almost purely serous, which is why mumps-swollen parotids matter for saliva's watery part.
levels.college:
**Oral mucosa** has three types:
- **Masticatory** (gingiva, hard palate): keratinized or parakeratinized stratified squamous epithelium firmly bound to periosteum, forming a **mucoperiosteum**.
- **Lining** (lips, cheeks, soft palate, ventral tongue): non-keratinized, over a loose submucosa with minor salivary glands.
- **Specialized** (dorsal tongue): papillae and taste buds.

**Tongue.** Intrinsic skeletal muscle bundles run longitudinally, transversely and vertically. **Foliate papillae** on the lateral margins join filiform, fungiform and circumvallate types. Circumvallate papillae sit in moats flushed by serous **von Ebner glands**, which clear tastants. **Taste buds** are pale, barrel-shaped intraepithelial clusters opening at a **taste pore**. They contain type I (glia-like), type II (receptor cells for sweet, bitter and umami via GPCRs) and type III (sour, with synapses) cells, plus basal stem cells. Cells turn over roughly every 10 days.

**Tooth.**
- **Enamel**: acellular, built from **enamel rods (prisms)** of hydroxyapatite. Ameloblasts derive from oral **ectoderm**. On routine decalcified slides enamel dissolves, leaving an empty space.
- **Dentin**: tubular, made by **odontoblasts** (from **neural crest** ectomesenchyme). Their processes extend into **dentinal tubules**, and the cell bodies line the pulp. An unmineralized **predentin** layer sits next to them.
- **Pulp**: loose connective tissue, vessels and nerves entering at the apical foramen.
- **Periodontium**: cementum, periodontal ligament (with **Sharpey fibers**) and alveolar bone, forming a fibrous joint called a **gomphosis**.

**Salivary glands** are compound tubuloacinar glands. Their duct system is the key to identifying them:
- **Acini**, then **intercalated ducts** (low cuboidal), then **striated ducts** (columnar, with basal mitochondrial striations that pump ions), then **excretory ducts**.
- **Myoepithelial cells** squeeze acini.
- **Parotid**: serous, with fat cells. **Submandibular**: mixed, mostly serous, with **serous demilunes**. **Sublingual**: mostly mucous.
- Striated ducts reabsorb Na+ and Cl- and secrete K+ and HCO3-, so final saliva is **hypotonic**.
levels.phd:
**Mucosal heterogeneity.** Keratinized gingival and palatal epithelium shows stratum basale, spinosum, granulosum and corneum, expressing keratins K1/K10. Non-keratinized buccal epithelium expresses K4/K13 and has a thicker, more permeable surface. Oral wounds heal faster and with less scarring than skin. This has been linked to a constitutively primed transcriptional state in oral keratinocytes, including SOX2 and PITX1 networks reported by Iglesias-Bartolome and colleagues (2018).

**Taste transduction.** Type II cells express **T1R2/T1R3** (sweet), **T1R1/T1R3** (umami) or T2Rs (bitter), coupled to gustducin, PLCβ2, IP3 and TRPM5. They lack conventional synapses and release ATP through **CALHM1/3 channels** onto P2X2/P2X3 afferents. Type III cells detect sour via the proton channel **OTOP1** and form classical serotonergic synapses. Salt is detected partly through ENaC.

**Odontogenesis.** Tooth development is a model of reciprocal epithelial-mesenchymal signaling. The enamel organ passes through bud, cap and bell stages. The **enamel knot** is a signaling center expressing Shh, FGFs, BMPs and Wnts, and it patterns cusps. Inner enamel epithelium induces neural-crest mesenchyme to become odontoblasts, which in turn trigger ameloblast differentiation. Mature enamel is about 96% mineral by weight. Ameloblasts secrete amelogenin and enamelin; Tomes' processes shape the rods; MMP20 and KLK4 then remove the matrix protein. The **Hertwig epithelial root sheath** guides root formation, and its remnants persist as the **epithelial rests of Malassez**.

**Salivary secretion.** Acinar fluid secretion follows a two-stage model (Thaysen). Muscarinic M3 stimulation raises intracellular Ca2+ and opens apical **TMEM16A** Cl- channels. NKCC1 loads Cl- basolaterally, and water follows through **aquaporin-5**, producing an isotonic primary fluid. Ducts then modify it, using CFTR and ENaC, into hypotonic saliva. Parasympathetic input drives copious watery flow. Sympathetic β-adrenergic input via cAMP drives protein (amylase) exocytosis. The **parotid** receives parasympathetic fibers via CN IX and the otic ganglion; the submandibular and sublingual glands via CN VII, the chorda tympani and the submandibular ganglion.

**Controversy.** Whether serous demilunes are real or an immersion-fixation artifact is debated. Rapid-freezing studies (Yamashina and colleagues) suggest serous cells actually line the acinar lumen alongside mucous cells, and conventional fixation swells mucous cells and pushes serous cells to the periphery.
levels.expert:
**Diagnostic histopathology.** Salivary tumors arise most often in the parotid, but a submandibular mass is more likely malignant, and a minor salivary gland mass is more likely still. **Pleomorphic adenoma**, the commonest, mixes ductal and myoepithelial cells in chondromyxoid stroma. Its incomplete capsule with pseudopodia explains why enucleation leads to recurrence. **Warthin tumor** shows bilayered oncocytic epithelium over lymphoid stroma and is strongly smoking-associated. **Mucoepidermoid carcinoma** is often driven by a CRTC1::MAML2 fusion. **Adenoid cystic carcinoma** (MYB::NFIB) is notorious for **perineural invasion**. Neurosurgeons and skull-base teams meet it tracking along V2/V3 into the cavernous sinus, so nerve margins matter.

**Iatrogenic and pharmacologic injury.** Radiotherapy for head and neck cancer destroys serous acini and progenitors, causing chronic xerostomia, rampant caries and osteoradionecrosis risk. Submandibular-sparing techniques and IMRT reduce this. Anticholinergic load (antimuscarinics, tricyclics, many antihistamines) is the commonest cause of dry mouth in practice. Muscarinic agonists such as pilocarpine and cevimeline need residual acinar tissue to work. Antiresorptives (bisphosphonates, denosumab) can cause **medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw**, and histology shows non-vital bone colonized by Actinomyces. **Sjögren disease** biopsy of minor labial glands uses a **focus score**: one or more foci of 50 or more lymphocytes per 4 mm² supports the diagnosis.

**Oral mucosa.** Leukoplakia is clinical, not histological. Dysplasia grading predicts progression imperfectly, and HPV-driven oropharyngeal carcinoma (p16-positive) arises from tonsillar crypt epithelium, not oral surface mucosa.

**Pitfalls on slides.** Decalcified sections show no enamel; ground sections keep enamel but lose soft tissue. Pancreas can mimic parotid, but it lacks striated ducts and has centroacinar cells and islets.

**Frontiers.** Salivary glands are a sensitive, noninvasive biofluid source. They are also a target of SARS-CoV-2, since ACE2 and TMPRSS2 are expressed in ducts and acini. Gene therapy with AAV2 encoding aquaporin-1 into irradiated parotids (Baum, NIDCR) restored flow in some patients. Dental-pulp stem cells and tooth bioengineering via recombined epithelial-mesenchymal germs remain experimental, and enamel regeneration is the hardest open problem because ameloblasts are gone after eruption.

keyPoints: Oral mucosa is stratified squamous: keratinized where chewing forces are high, non-keratinized elsewhere
Filiform papillae lack taste buds; fungiform, foliate and circumvallate papillae carry them
Enamel (from ameloblasts, ectoderm) cannot regrow; dentin comes from neural-crest odontoblasts throughout life
Salivary ducts run acinus, intercalated, striated, then excretory; striated ducts make saliva hypotonic
Parotid is serous, submandibular is mixed, sublingual is mostly mucous
Parasympathetic input gives watery saliva; sympathetic input boosts protein secretion

test.q: Which epithelium lines the oral cavity?
test.explain: Many-layered squamous epithelium resists the abrasion of chewing. Simple columnar lines the stomach and intestine, not the mouth.

test.q: Which tongue papillae are most numerous but lack taste buds?
test.explain: Filiform papillae are pointed and give grip but carry no taste buds.

test.q: Which cells produce dentin?
test.explain: Odontoblasts line the pulp and send processes into dentinal tubules. Ameloblasts make enamel instead.

test.q: Why can enamel not repair itself after a tooth erupts?
choices: Its blood supply is cut off
test.explain: Ameloblasts disappear once the tooth erupts, so no cells remain to make new enamel.

test.q: Which salivary gland is almost purely serous?
test.explain: The parotid secretes watery, enzyme-rich saliva. The sublingual gland is mostly mucous.

test.q: Which duct segment has basal striations from mitochondria and modifies ion content?
test.explain: Striated ducts pump ions, reabsorbing Na+ and Cl-, which makes saliva hypotonic.

test.q: Final saliva compared with plasma is:
test.explain: Ducts reabsorb more salt than water, so saliva ends up hypotonic. The primary acinar fluid is the part that starts isotonic.

test.q: Cells that squeeze salivary acini to expel secretion are:
test.explain: Contractile myoepithelial cells wrap around acini and help push saliva into the ducts.

test.q: Fibers anchoring cementum to alveolar bone are found in the:
test.explain: The periodontal ligament, with Sharpey fibers, links cementum to bone in a gomphosis joint.

test.q: What salivary enzyme starts the digestion of starch?
test.explain: Serous cells secrete amylase, which begins breaking starch down in the mouth.

test.q: The large papillae arranged in a V at the back of the tongue are called ___ papillae.
test.explain: There are about 8-12 of them, with many taste buds in their trenches.

test.q: Enamel is made mostly of the mineral ___.
test.explain: Enamel is about 96% hydroxyapatite, which makes it the hardest tissue in the body.

kidTest.q: What is the hardest stuff in your body?
kidTest.explain: Enamel, the outer layer of teeth, is harder than bone.

kidTest.q: What are the little bumps on your tongue called?
kidTest.explain: Papillae are the tongue bumps, and some of them hold taste buds.

kidTest.q: What is in the middle of a tooth?
kidTest.explain: The pulp holds nerves and blood vessels.

kidTest.q: What do salivary glands look like?
kidTest.explain: Each 'grape' makes saliva that flows into tiny tubes leading to your mouth.

kidTest.q: Clusters of cells that let you taste food are called taste b _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Taste buds sense sweet, salty, sour, bitter and savory.

advancedTest.q: A patient lacking CALHM1/3 function would most likely lose which tastes?
advancedTest.explain: Type II cells release ATP through CALHM1/3, and these cells detect sweet, bitter and umami. Sour uses type III cells with OTOP1 and conventional synapses.

advancedTest.q: Pilocarpine fails to improve dry mouth after high-dose head and neck radiotherapy mainly because:
choices: Striated ducts now secrete too much water
Acinar tissue it would stimulate has been destroyed
Muscarinic receptors on ducts are blocked by scarring
Sympathetic fibers override the parasympathetic input
advancedTest.explain: Muscarinic agonists need surviving acini to act on. Radiation destroys serous acini and progenitors.

advancedTest.q: A pathologist must tell parotid from pancreas on a small biopsy. The most useful feature is:
advancedTest.explain: Both glands have serous zymogen-rich acini. Striated ducts point to parotid, while islets and centroacinar cells point to pancreas.

advancedTest.q: Rapid-freezing studies challenge serous demilunes by suggesting that:
choices: Demilunes are a feature of parotid tissue
Serous cells are absent from mixed acini
Fixation swells mucous cells, displacing serous cells
Demilunes are mucous cells stained abnormally
advancedTest.explain: With rapid freezing, serous cells line the lumen alongside mucous cells. Conventional immersion fixation swells mucous cells and creates the crescent appearance.

lessons.title: Esophagus & Stomach: Gastric Glands and Cell Types

levels.kid:
Your food takes a slide down a long tube called the **esophagus**. Its lining is tough and made of many flat layers stacked like a pile of pancakes. That way, crunchy chips don't scrape it raw.

At the bottom is the **stomach**, a stretchy bag that mixes food like a washing machine. Its walls are full of tiny pits. Inside each pit live special helper cells.

- Some make **acid**, strong enough to kill germs.
- Some make a juice that starts breaking down meat.
- Some make slimy **mucus**, a coat that keeps the stomach from digesting itself!

Under a microscope, scientists can see all these different cells, each doing its own job.
levels.hs:
Every part of the gut tube has the same four layers: the inner **mucosa** (lining), the **submucosa** (blood vessels and glands), the **muscularis externa** (muscle that moves food), and an outer covering. Each segment changes these layers to suit its job.

The **esophagus** carries food from throat to stomach. It is lined by **nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium**: many layers of flat cells that resist rubbing. Its muscle is skeletal (voluntary) in the upper third and smooth in the lower third, with a mix in between.

At the **gastroesophageal junction**, the lining switches abruptly to simple columnar epithelium. The stomach surface is dotted with **gastric pits** that open into **gastric glands**. Key cell types in these glands:
- **Surface mucous cells**: make a thick mucus and bicarbonate layer that protects the lining.
- **Parietal cells**: make hydrochloric acid and **intrinsic factor**, which is needed to absorb vitamin B12.
- **Chief cells**: make **pepsinogen**, which acid turns into pepsin, an enzyme that digests protein.
- **Enteroendocrine cells**: release hormones such as gastrin.

Real example: in **GERD** (chronic acid reflux), acid repeatedly burns the lower esophagus. Over time the lining can change into a stomach- or intestine-like columnar lining called **Barrett's esophagus**, which raises the risk of cancer.
levels.college:
**Esophagus.** Mucosa: nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium, lamina propria, and a prominent muscularis mucosae. The submucosa contains **esophageal glands proper**, which secrete lubricating mucus. Near the stomach, **esophageal cardiac glands** sit in the lamina propria. The muscularis externa shifts from skeletal muscle (upper third) to mixed, then smooth muscle (lower third). Most of the esophagus has an **adventitia**; the short abdominal segment has a serosa.

**Stomach regions.** Cardia, fundus, body, and pyloric antrum. When empty, the mucosa forms longitudinal folds called **rugae**. All regions share a surface of simple columnar **surface mucous cells**, which have no goblet cells. These sit over **gastric pits (foveolae)**. The glands differ by region:
- **Cardiac glands**: coiled, mostly mucous.
- **Fundic (oxyntic) glands**: in the fundus and body. They are straight, with shallow pits about a quarter of the mucosal depth and long glands.
- **Pyloric glands**: deep pits about half the mucosal depth, coiled mucous glands, and abundant G cells.

**Fundic gland anatomy and cells:**
- **Isthmus**: home to stem cells, which renew the surface cells every 3-5 days.
- **Neck**: **mucous neck cells** that secrete soluble mucus. Parietal cells are dense here.
- **Base**: **chief cells**, basophilic because of abundant rough ER, with apical zymogen granules of pepsinogen and gastric lipase.
- **Parietal (oxyntic) cells**: large and eosinophilic, often described as "fried egg" cells. They are packed with mitochondria and have intracellular canaliculi. They secrete HCl and intrinsic factor.
- **Enteroendocrine cells**: G cells (gastrin), D cells (somatostatin), and ECL cells (histamine).

**Acid control.** Three signals drive acid secretion: acetylcholine (vagal M3 receptors), gastrin (CCK2 receptors), and histamine (H2 receptors). All converge on the **H+/K+-ATPase**. Gastrin acts largely by stimulating ECL cells to release histamine. This is why H2 blockers and proton-pump inhibitors are both effective.

**Muscularis externa.** The stomach adds a third, inner oblique layer to the usual inner circular and outer longitudinal layers. The circular layer thickens to form the pyloric sphincter.
levels.phd:
The **parietal cell** is a model of membrane remodeling. At rest, H+/K+-ATPase (ATP4A/ATP4B) is sequestered in **tubulovesicles**. When stimulated, cAMP (from H2 receptors) and Ca2+ (from M3 and CCK2 receptors) trigger fusion of these vesicles with the apical canalicular membrane. Ezrin phosphorylation by PKA is a key step. This expands the apical surface several-fold, and electron micrographs show dense microvilli lining the canaliculi. The pump exchanges H+ for K+ electroneutrally, and apical KCNQ1 and CLIC/CFTR-family channels recycle K+ and supply Cl-. The resulting gradient reaches about a million-fold (lumen pH near 1 versus cytosol about 7.2). Basolaterally, the HCO3-/Cl- exchanger AE2 exports bicarbonate, producing the postprandial **alkaline tide**. Intrinsic factor (GIF) in humans comes from parietal cells; in rodents it comes from chief cells.

Proton-pump inhibitors are prodrugs. They are protonated and concentrated in the acidic canaliculus, rearrange into sulfenamides, and covalently bind cysteines (for example Cys813) on actively cycling pumps. This explains why they work best when taken before meals.

**Gland lineage dynamics.** Isthmal stem and progenitor cells generate:
- pit cells that migrate upward;
- parietal cells that migrate bidirectionally and live for months;
- mucous neck cells that mature into chief cells as they descend.

The neck-to-chief transition depends on the transcription factor **MIST1 (BHLHA15)**. Lineage tracing by Clevers' group identified Lgr5+ cells at antral gland bases and Troy+ reserve chief cells in the corpus.

**Metaplasia.** When parietal cells are lost, for example through *Helicobacter pylori* infection, autoimmune gastritis, or experimentally with DMP-777 or L-635, chief cells transdifferentiate. They become **SPEM (spasmolytic polypeptide-expressing metaplasia)**, marked by TFF2 and GSII lectin binding. The process resembles **paligenosis**, a conserved program of autodegradation followed by re-entry into the cell cycle (Mills). Whether SPEM truly leads to intestinal metaplasia and adenocarcinoma, or simply marks a field of risk, remains debated.

In the **esophagus**, the squamous basal layer is renewed by p63+ progenitors. The cell of origin of Barrett's columnar epithelium is still contested. Candidates include gastric cardia progenitors migrating upward, transitional basal cells at the squamocolumnar junction, residual embryonic cells, and submucosal gland ducts.
levels.expert:
**Reading the biopsy.** Gastric pathology hinges on recognizing which glands belong where. Antral and corpus mucosa look alike at low power, so pathologists rely on clues:
- Gastrin immunostaining highlights G cells and marks a biopsy as antral.
- **Pseudopyloric (pyloric) metaplasia** of the corpus is a sign of chronic atrophic gastritis.
- In **autoimmune gastritis**, anti-parietal cell and anti-intrinsic factor antibodies destroy oxyntic mucosa while the antrum is spared. Loss of acid causes hypergastrinemia, which drives linear and nodular **ECL-cell hyperplasia** and type 1 neuroendocrine tumors. Pernicious anemia from B12 deficiency can present neurologically with subacute combined degeneration, a reason neurosurgeons and neurologists should know gastric histology.

**Carcinogenesis.** The **Correa cascade** runs: chronic gastritis → atrophy → intestinal metaplasia (goblet cells, CDX2) → dysplasia → intestinal-type adenocarcinoma. The **OLGA/OLGIM** staging systems turn biopsy findings into a risk estimate. Diffuse-type, signet-ring cancer follows a separate pathway, classically through CDH1 (E-cadherin) loss in hereditary diffuse gastric cancer. In these families, the earliest lesions are in situ signet-ring foci too small for endoscopy to reliably detect.

**Long-term acid suppression.** Chronic PPI use produces **parietal cell protrusions** and oxyntic gland dilatation, and can cause fundic gland polyps. These polyps usually lack the APC/β-catenin-driven dysplasia seen in familial adenomatous polyposis.

**Barrett's esophagus.** Guidelines differ. The ACG requires goblet cells for diagnosis; the BSG accepts columnar mucosa without them. Endoscopic risk tools and nonendoscopic sampling devices (Cytosponge with TFF3 staining) are reshaping surveillance. **Eosinophilic esophagitis** is diagnosed partly by a peak count of at least 15 eosinophils per high-power field, with basal zone hyperplasia and dilated intercellular spaces.

**Frontier work.**
- Single-cell atlases of human stomach and esophagus resolve isthmal progenitors and transitional basal cells at the gastroesophageal junction.
- Gastric organoids derived from Lgr5+ or pluripotent stem cells (Wells, McCracken) model *H. pylori* CagA injection and host responses.
- Potassium-competitive acid blockers such as vonoprazan block the H+/K+-ATPase reversibly without needing acid activation. This sidesteps the PPI requirement for actively cycling pumps.

**Open questions.** Is SPEM a precursor of cancer or only a bystander? What is the true cell of origin of Barrett's epithelium? And can intestinal metaplasia reverse after *H. pylori* eradication?

keyPoints: Esophagus: nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium; muscle shifts from skeletal to smooth
GE junction switches abruptly to simple columnar mucus-secreting epithelium
Parietal cells secrete HCl via H+/K+-ATPase and intrinsic factor for B12
Chief cells secrete pepsinogen; mucous neck cells and surface cells make mucus
ACh, gastrin and histamine converge on acid secretion; gastrin acts via ECL histamine
Chronic injury causes metaplasia: Barrett's esophagus, SPEM, intestinal metaplasia

test.q: What epithelium lines most of the human esophagus?
test.explain: Multiple flat, nonkeratinized layers resist abrasion from swallowed food. Keratinized epithelium is found in skin, not the esophagus.

test.q: Which gastric cell secretes hydrochloric acid?
test.explain: Parietal (oxyntic) cells pump H+ into the lumen using the H+/K+-ATPase. Chief cells make pepsinogen instead.

test.q: Chief cells stain basophilic mainly because they contain abundant:
test.explain: Ribosome-rich rough ER makes the cytoplasm take up basic dyes. Abundant mitochondria are what make parietal cells eosinophilic.

test.q: What is the main role of intrinsic factor?
test.explain: Intrinsic factor from parietal cells binds vitamin B12 so it can be absorbed further down the gut. Acid, not intrinsic factor, activates pepsinogen.

test.q: Gastrin promotes acid secretion largely by stimulating which cells?
test.explain: Gastrin triggers ECL cells to release histamine, which then acts on parietal cell H2 receptors. D cells release somatostatin, which inhibits acid.

test.q: In the lower third of the esophagus, the muscularis externa consists of:
test.explain: The upper third is skeletal, the middle is mixed, and the lower third is smooth muscle.

test.q: Compared with fundic glands, pyloric glands have:
choices: Shallower pits and more chief cells
Deeper pits and abundant G cells
Many parietal cells at the base
test.explain: Pyloric (antral) glands have deep pits, mucous glands, and many gastrin-producing G cells. Normal stomach has no goblet cells.

test.q: Barrett's esophagus is a change from squamous to:
test.explain: Chronic acid reflux causes metaplasia to a stomach- or intestine-like columnar lining, which raises cancer risk.

test.q: What unusual feature does the stomach's muscularis externa have?
test.explain: The stomach adds an inner oblique layer to the usual circular and longitudinal layers, which helps it churn food.

test.q: Which inactive enzyme do chief cells secrete, which acid converts into a protein-digesting enzyme?
test.explain: Acid cleaves pepsinogen into active pepsin.

test.q: The longitudinal folds of an empty stomach's mucosa are called ___.
test.explain: Rugae flatten out as the stomach fills and stretches.

test.q: Proton-pump inhibitors block the H+/K+-___ in parietal cells.
test.explain: The H+/K+-ATPase is the final common step of acid secretion.

kidTest.q: What is the esophagus?
choices: A gland that makes your saliva
A bag that stores your food
A tube from throat to stomach
kidTest.explain: Food slides down the esophagus to reach the stomach.

kidTest.q: Why is the esophagus lining made of many layers?
choices: To help it soak up water
So rough food doesn't scrape it
kidTest.explain: Stacked layers protect the lining like a pile of pancakes.

kidTest.q: What does stomach acid help do?
kidTest.explain: Strong acid kills germs and helps break down food.

kidTest.q: Why does the stomach make slimy mucus?
choices: To help it digest food faster
kidTest.explain: Mucus coats the lining so the stomach doesn't digest itself.

kidTest.q: The stomach has tiny holes in its wall where helper cells live. They are called p _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Gastric pits lead down into glands full of helper cells.

advancedTest.q: Why are proton-pump inhibitors most effective when taken before a meal?
choices: They bind pumps that are actively cycling and need acid activation
Food increases the number of chief cells making pepsinogen
They need food to be absorbed from the gut
Meals block histamine from reaching the H2 receptor
advancedTest.explain: PPIs are acid-activated prodrugs that covalently bind active pumps in the canaliculus. Meal-stimulated secretion maximizes the number of such pumps.

advancedTest.q: A biopsy shows corpus atrophy with ECL-cell hyperplasia and the antrum spared. The most likely cause is:
choices: Long-term use of H2 receptor blockers
advancedTest.explain: Autoimmune loss of parietal cells removes acid feedback, so G cells oversecrete gastrin, which drives ECL hyperplasia. The antrum is characteristically spared.

advancedTest.q: Ablating parietal cells with DMP-777 leads chief cells to form SPEM. This best shows that:
choices: Parietal cells turn over within a few days
Chief cells come from parietal cells
Acid is required for chief cell survival
Mature chief cells can reprogram after injury
advancedTest.explain: Chief cells transdifferentiate through a paligenosis-like program after parietal cell loss. Parietal cells actually live for months, not days.

advancedTest.q: Why can vonoprazan suppress acid without depending on pump activation?
choices: It blocks H2 receptors at the basolateral membrane
It inhibits gastrin release from antral G cells
It competes with K+ at the pump without needing acid conversion
It covalently binds cysteines on resting tubulovesicles
advancedTest.explain: Potassium-competitive acid blockers bind reversibly and do not need acid activation, unlike PPI prodrugs that form covalent bonds with active pumps.

lessons.title: Small & Large Intestine: Villi, Crypts & Colon

levels.kid:
Your intestines are a long, folded tube where food gets soaked up into your body.

The **small intestine** is covered inside with millions of tiny finger shapes called **villi**. They make the inside feel like a fuzzy towel. A fuzzy towel soaks up more water than a smooth one, and villi soak up more food the same way.

Between the fingers are little pockets called **crypts**. New cells are born there and slowly move up. Old cells fall off the tips after a few days, like leaves dropping from a tree.

The **large intestine** has no fingers. It is smoother, with lots of slimy helper cells. Its job is to take back water and make the leftovers slippery so they slide out.
levels.hs:
After the stomach, food enters the **small intestine** (duodenum, jejunum, ileum) and then the **large intestine** (colon and rectum). Under a microscope, both have the same four gut-wall layers: **mucosa**, **submucosa**, **muscularis externa** and **serosa**. The inner lining shows how each part fits its job.

The small intestine absorbs nutrients, so it has three levels of folding to increase surface area:
- **Plicae circulares**: large circular folds of mucosa and submucosa.
- **Villi**: finger-like projections of mucosa, about 0.5-1 mm tall.
- **Microvilli**: tiny projections on each absorptive cell, forming the **brush border**.

Together these expand the surface roughly 600-fold compared with a smooth tube.

Between the villi are **crypts of Lieberkühn**, tubular glands where **stem cells** divide. New cells migrate up the villus and are shed at the tip after about 3-5 days, so the lining is replaced constantly.

Key cells: **enterocytes** (absorb), **goblet cells** (make mucus), **Paneth cells** (release antibacterial proteins) and **enteroendocrine cells** (release hormones).

The **colon** absorbs water and salts and has no villi. Its mucosa is flat, with straight, deep crypts packed with goblet cells. Its outer muscle forms three bands called **taeniae coli**.

Example: in **celiac disease**, gluten triggers an immune reaction that flattens the villi. Absorption drops, causing weight loss and anemia.
levels.college:
**Shared wall plan.** The mucosa (epithelium, lamina propria, muscularis mucosae), submucosa (with Meissner's plexus), muscularis externa (inner circular, outer longitudinal, with Auerbach's myenteric plexus between) and serosa or adventitia.

**Small intestine amplification.** Plicae circulares (permanent submucosal folds), villi (mucosal projections with a central **lacteal**, capillaries and smooth muscle), and microvilli (actin cores, glycocalyx carrying disaccharidases and peptidases). The epithelium is simple columnar.

**Crypt-villus unit cell types:**
- **Enterocytes**: absorb sugars (SGLT1, GLUT5, GLUT2), amino acids and lipids. Lipids are repackaged into **chylomicrons**, which enter lacteals.
- **Goblet cells**: secrete MUC2 mucin; they become more numerous distally.
- **Paneth cells**: crypt base, bright eosinophilic granules containing lysozyme and α-defensins; most abundant in the ileum.
- **Enteroendocrine cells**: I cells (CCK), S cells (secretin), K cells (GIP), L cells (GLP-1).
- **M cells**: overlie Peyer's patches and sample antigens.
- **Tuft cells**: chemosensory cells that sense parasites.

**Distinguishing segments on a slide:**
- **Duodenum**: **Brunner's glands** in the submucosa secrete alkaline mucus that neutralizes gastric acid.
- **Jejunum**: tall, leaf-like villi and prominent plicae; no Brunner's glands or Peyer's patches.
- **Ileum**: **Peyer's patches** (aggregated lymphoid follicles), shorter villi, more goblet cells.

**Large intestine.** No villi and no plicae. Straight crypts are dominated by goblet cells, with colonocytes absorbing water and Na+ through ENaC. Colonocytes rely on butyrate from bacterial fermentation as fuel. The longitudinal muscle is gathered into **taeniae coli**, producing haustra; fatty **appendices epiploicae** hang from the serosa. The appendix has abundant lymphoid follicles. At the **anorectal junction**, simple columnar epithelium changes to stratified squamous at the pectinate line.

**Renewal.** LGR5+ stem cells at the crypt base drive turnover in about 3-5 days. Paneth cells are the exception: they migrate downward and live for weeks.
levels.phd:
**Stem cell hierarchy.** Barker and Clevers (2007) used lineage tracing to identify **LGR5+ crypt base columnar (CBC) cells** interspersed between Paneth cells as multipotent, self-renewing stem cells. A single LGR5+ cell can generate self-organizing **organoids** in Matrigel (Sato et al., 2009). A slower **"+4" population** (Bmi1, Hopx, Tert markers) and dedifferentiating progenitors can repopulate the crypt after LGR5+ cells are ablated. This shows that "stemness" is a state defined by the niche rather than a fixed identity.

**Niche signaling:**
- **Wnt**: comes from Paneth cells (Wnt3) and subepithelial telocytes/trophocytes. R-spondin binding to LGR4/5 inhibits RNF43/ZNRF3, stabilizing Frizzled. Wnt is high at the crypt base.
- **BMP**: high toward the villus, opposed by crypt-base noggin/gremlin. This drives differentiation.
- **Notch**: Paneth cells present Dll1/Dll4. High Notch (via Hes1) favors the absorptive fate; low Notch derepresses **Atoh1 (Math1)**, favoring secretory fates (goblet, Paneth, enteroendocrine via Neurog3).
- **EGF** from Paneth cells supports proliferation.

Cells are **monoclonal per crypt** through neutral drift: stem cells compete stochastically until one clone fixes. Villi, by contrast, are polyclonal and receive cells from several crypts.

**Absorption mechanics.** SGLT1 couples Na+-glucose cotransport to the basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase gradient, the basis of oral rehydration therapy. Lipid digestion produces micelle uptake via CD36/NPC1L1, re-esterification in the smooth ER, and MTP-dependent chylomicron assembly. Absence of the MTP protein causes abetalipoproteinemia, in which enterocytes appear lipid-laden. The ileum specifically absorbs B12-intrinsic factor (via cubilin) and bile acids (via ASBT).

**Barrier.** Tight junctions (claudins, occludin, ZO-1) regulate the paracellular route. Claudin-2 forms leaky cation pores in the crypts. The colon has a two-layer MUC2 mucus: the inner layer is firmly attached and almost sterile, the outer layer is loose and colonized (Johansson and Hansson). The small intestine has a single, discontinuous layer, so antimicrobial peptides such as RegIIIγ keep bacteria at a distance.

**Celiac histology** is graded by the **Marsh-Oberhuber** system: intraepithelial lymphocytosis (more than 25 IELs per 100 enterocytes), then crypt hyperplasia, then villous atrophy. This progression reflects IL-15-driven cytotoxic IELs.
levels.expert:
**Biopsy pitfalls.** Villus:crypt ratio (normally about 3-5:1) is only interpretable in well-oriented sections. Tangential cuts mimic blunting. Brunner's glands and lymphoid aggregates make the duodenal bulb flatter, so guidelines recommend separate bulb and distal duodenal samples. Raised IELs with normal architecture (Marsh 1) are nonspecific: causes include NSAIDs, *H. pylori*, infection and autoimmunity. Serology (tTG-IgA) and HLA-DQ2/DQ8 testing provide context. Also consider sprue mimics: olmesartan enteropathy, common variable immunodeficiency (look for absent plasma cells) and tropical sprue.

**Inflammatory bowel disease.** Chronicity is shown by **crypt architectural distortion** (branching, dropout), **basal plasmacytosis** and **Paneth cell metaplasia** in the left colon. Ulcerative colitis is continuous and mucosal. Crohn disease is patchy and transmural, with non-caseating granulomas found in only a minority of biopsies. Ileal Paneth cell dysfunction connects NOD2 and ATG16L1 risk alleles to Crohn disease through defective defensin secretion and autophagy.

**Neoplasia.** In the **adenoma-carcinoma sequence**, APC loss produces constitutive β-catenin signaling: the crypt behaves as if it were in a permanent Wnt-high state. KRAS and TP53 mutations follow. Sessile serrated lesions take a separate BRAF/CIMP pathway. On biopsy, these show dilated, L- or boot-shaped crypt bases. The "bottom-up" versus "top-down" debate about adenoma origin is largely settled toward stem cell-driven origin. Clevers' work showed that LGR5+ cells are the cells of origin after Apc deletion.

**Other cell findings.** Abetalipoproteinemia produces vacuolated enterocytes. **Whipple disease** causes the lamina propria to fill with PAS-positive foamy macrophages; *Tropheryma whipplei* is confirmed by PCR. Microvillus inclusion disease (MYO5B mutations) appears as CD10-positive apical inclusions, and electron microscopy is diagnostic.

**Frontiers.** Patient-derived organoids predict CFTR modulator response through a forskolin-induced swelling assay and are being tested to guide colorectal cancer chemotherapy. Single-cell atlases have revealed BEST4+/OTOP2+ colonocytes and distinct fibroblast niches. Fetal-like "revival stem cells" (Clu+) appear during injury repair. Open questions include whether cell plasticity fuels cancer relapse after targeted therapy, and how microbial metabolites shape crypt fate. Butyrate, for instance, inhibits stem cell proliferation, which explains why stem cells sit at the base of colonic crypts, away from it.

Crypts of Lieberkühn hold LGR5+ stem cells; the lining renews every 3-5 days
Brunner's glands mark the duodenum; Peyer's patches mark the ileum

lessons.title: Liver: Lobules, Acini & Hepatocytes

levels.kid:
Your liver is a big, soft organ tucked under your ribs on the right side. It is like a busy cleaning and cooking factory for your blood.

Under a microscope, the liver looks like a honeycomb made of tiny six-sided shapes called **lobules**. At each corner of a shape there are three little tubes. Two bring blood in. One carries away **bile**, a green juice that helps you digest fat.

Blood flows from the corners toward the middle of each shape. It squeezes past rows of hard-working cells called **hepatocytes**. They pull out food and clean away harmful stuff, a bit like workers on a conveyor belt. Then the blood leaves through a vein in the center.
levels.hs:
The liver is the body's largest internal organ, and under the microscope it has a strikingly regular pattern.

**Hepatocytes** are the main liver cells. They are large, with one or two round nuclei. They store sugar as glycogen, make blood proteins like albumin and clotting factors, produce **bile**, and break down drugs and toxins.

The liver gets blood from two sources:
- The **hepatic artery** brings oxygen-rich blood.
- The **portal vein** brings nutrient-rich blood straight from the intestines.

Under the microscope, liver tissue is organized into **classic lobules**: roughly six-sided units with a **central vein** in the middle. At the corners sit **portal triads**, each holding a branch of the hepatic artery, a branch of the portal vein, and a **bile duct**.

Hepatocytes line up in plates, one or two cells thick, that radiate from the central vein like spokes on a wheel. Between the plates run leaky capillaries called **sinusoids**. Blood flows inward from the triads, through the sinusoids, to the central vein. Bile flows the opposite way, outward toward the bile ducts.

One real example: in pigs the lobules are outlined by thick connective tissue, so the hexagons are easy to see. In human liver the borders are faint, and you find lobules by locating central veins and triads.
levels.college:
The liver's microscopic structure can be described with three models, each emphasizing a different function.

**Classic lobule** (blood drainage): hexagonal, centered on the **central (terminal hepatic) vein**, with **portal triads** at the corners. Each triad contains a hepatic arteriole, portal venule and bile ductule (lined by cuboidal cholangiocytes), plus lymphatics.

**Portal lobule** (bile secretion): triangular, centered on a triad, with three central veins at its points. It emphasizes the exocrine drainage of bile.

**Liver acinus of Rappaport** (metabolism): diamond-shaped, with its short axis along the border between two lobules and central veins at its two tips. It is divided into zones by distance from the incoming blood:
- **Zone 1 (periportal)**: most oxygen and nutrients; gluconeogenesis, beta-oxidation, urea synthesis.
- **Zone 2**: intermediate.
- **Zone 3 (centrilobular)**: least oxygen; glycolysis, lipogenesis, high cytochrome P450 activity. It is the most vulnerable to ischemia and drug toxicity.

**Sinusoids** are discontinuous capillaries with fenestrated endothelium and no true basement membrane. They receive mixed arterial and portal blood. Between endothelium and hepatocytes lies the **space of Disse**, where microvilli on the hepatocytes contact plasma directly.

Key sinusoidal cells:
- **Kupffer cells**: resident macrophages that clear gut-derived bacteria, particles and old red cells.
- **Hepatic stellate (Ito) cells**: in the space of Disse; store vitamin A.

**Hepatocytes** are polarized epithelial cells. Their basolateral (sinusoidal) surface exchanges with blood. Their apical surfaces form **bile canaliculi**, tiny channels sealed by tight junctions. Bile flows from the canaliculi into the **canals of Hering**, then to bile ductules. The cytoplasm is rich in rough and smooth ER, mitochondria, glycogen and peroxisomes, and is often binucleate or polyploid. The liver as a whole is wrapped in **Glisson's capsule**.
levels.phd:
Hepatic architecture is a solution to a transport problem. About 75% of afferent flow comes from the portal vein and about 25% from the hepatic artery. The two mix in sinusoids and travel in series past roughly 15-25 hepatocytes before draining centrally. This produces steep gradients in oxygen, hormones and substrates. Rappaport's acinar model (1950s) captured this better than Kiernan's 1833 classic lobule, though modern 3D reconstructions suggest the lobule and acinus are complementary descriptions, not competing truths.

**Metabolic zonation** is actively maintained, not just a passive result of oxygen falling along the sinusoid. **Wnt/beta-catenin** signaling is high pericentrally, driven by Wnt2 and Wnt9b and R-spondin3 from central vein endothelium. It induces glutamine synthetase (expressed only in a ring of one to three cells around the central vein), CYP2E1 and CYP1A2. APC, a negative regulator of beta-catenin, is enriched periportally, along with Hedgehog and other signals that favor periportal programs. Ammonia handling shows the logic: periportal hepatocytes run the high-capacity, low-affinity urea cycle (carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I). Pericentral cells scavenge the remainder via high-affinity glutamine synthetase.

The **sinusoidal endothelium** has fenestrae of roughly 100-150 nm in diameter, clustered in sieve plates and lacking a diaphragm. This allows lipoproteins and chylomicron remnants to reach the space of Disse. In **capillarization**, fenestrae are lost and a basement membrane forms, impairing exchange.

**Stellate cells** store retinyl esters in lipid droplets. When activated by TGF-beta and PDGF, they lose those droplets, become myofibroblasts and deposit collagen I. This is the central cellular event in fibrosis.

Hepatocyte **polarity** is unusual. Rather than a single apical surface facing a lumen, each cell has several apical belts forming canaliculi with its neighbours. Bile acids are secreted by **BSEP (ABCB11)** and phospholipids by **MDR3 (ABCB4)**. Uptake occurs basolaterally via **NTCP** and **OATPs**. Hepatocytes are commonly polyploid (tetraploid, octoploid), a feature linked to stress tolerance.

Regeneration after two-thirds partial hepatectomy (Higgins and Anderson, 1931) mainly involves division of existing hepatocytes, not stem cells. Where the new cells come from in normal turnover is debated, with pericentral Axin2+ cells and zone 2 hepatocytes both proposed.
levels.expert:
Zonation translates directly into lesion patterns that pathologists and clinicians read:

- **Zone 3 necrosis** in acetaminophen (paracetamol) toxicity. Pericentral CYP2E1 and CYP1A2 generate the reactive metabolite **NAPQI**, and pericentral glutathione is depleted first. N-acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione. Zone 3 also bears **ischemic hepatitis** (shock liver) and congestive hepatopathy. In right heart failure, centrilobular congestion and necrosis produce the gross "nutmeg liver."
- **Zone 1 injury** occurs with some directly acting toxins delivered first to periportal cells. Examples are white phosphorus and ferrous sulfate, and periportal damage is also seen in eclampsia.
- **Interface hepatitis** at the limiting plate around portal tracts is the hallmark of autoimmune and chronic viral hepatitis. Its severity drives histologic grading.
- **Fibrosis staging** (METAVIR F0-F4; Ishak 0-6) tracks septa linking portal and central areas, ending in regenerative nodules (cirrhosis). In steatohepatitis, fibrosis classically begins as pericellular "chicken-wire" collagen in zone 3.

Useful stains include:
- **Masson trichrome** for collagen.
- **Reticulin** to judge plate thickness. Plates more than two cells thick raise concern for hepatocellular carcinoma.
- **PAS with and without diastase** to separate glycogen from the PAS-positive globules of alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.
- **Perls' Prussian blue** for iron. Iron accumulates periportally in hereditary hemochromatosis.
- **Glutamine synthetase immunostaining**, a zonation marker. Its "map-like" pattern identifies focal nodular hyperplasia, and diffuse staining suggests beta-catenin-activated adenoma.

Pitfalls: needle biopsies sample about 1/50,000 of the liver. At least 10-11 portal tracts are generally wanted for reliable staging. Subcapsular tissue can falsely suggest fibrosis.

Frontiers:
- **Spatial transcriptomics** (Halpern and Itzkovitz, 2017, using single-molecule FISH-anchored single-cell RNA-seq) showed that roughly half of hepatocyte genes are zonated. It revealed zonation of endothelial cells and stellate cells too.
- Treatment of fibrosis has advanced. Resmetirom, a thyroid hormone receptor-beta agonist, gained FDA accelerated approval in 2024 for MASH with fibrosis. This is the condition formerly called NASH, renamed in the 2023 nomenclature as MASLD/MASH.

Open questions remain. One is whether advanced fibrosis truly regresses at the architectural level. Another is how zonation is reprogrammed during regeneration and in organoids. Relevant to neurosurgery, **hepatic encephalopathy** links failed periportal and pericentral ammonia handling to astrocyte glutamine accumulation and brain swelling.

lessons.title: Pancreas & Gallbladder

levels.kid:
Your tummy has two helpers tucked beside it: the **pancreas** and the **gallbladder**.

The pancreas is like a busy kitchen. Most of it is made of tiny round rooms called **acini**. They cook up juices that chop food into tiny pieces. Sprinkled in between are little islands, like islands in a sea. These **islets** make **insulin**, a messenger that tells your body how to use sugar.

The gallbladder is a small squishy bag under the liver. It stores **bile**, a green juice that helps break up fat, a bit like soap breaks up grease on a plate. The gallbladder squeezes water out of bile to make it stronger. When you eat a fatty meal, it squeezes the bile into your gut.
levels.hs:
The **pancreas** is really two organs in one, and a microscope shows both.

- The **exocrine pancreas** (about 98% of its mass) is built from grape-like clusters called **acini**. Each acinar cell is shaped like a pyramid. Its base stains purple because it is packed with rough ER for making protein. Its tip is full of pink **zymogen granules**, which store inactive digestive enzymes. Ducts carry the juice to the duodenum.
- The **endocrine pancreas** is scattered pale patches called **islets of Langerhans** (about 1 to 2% of the mass). These release hormones straight into blood: **beta cells** make insulin and **alpha cells** make glucagon.

Enzymes are stored inactive so the pancreas does not digest itself. They switch on only in the gut. If they activate early, the result is **pancreatitis**.

The **gallbladder** stores and concentrates **bile** made by the liver. Its wall is simple: a lining of tall **simple columnar epithelium** thrown into folds, a lamina propria, a layer of smooth muscle, and an outer covering. Unlike the intestine, it has no muscularis mucosae and no submucosa. Its lining cells pump salt and water out, which concentrates the bile several-fold. The hormone **cholecystokinin (CCK)** makes the muscle contract after a fatty meal.

A real example: when bile becomes too concentrated, cholesterol can crystallize into **gallstones**.
levels.college:
**Exocrine pancreas.** This is a compound tubuloacinar serous gland, divided into lobules by thin septa.
- **Acinar cells** show classic polarity. The basal cytoplasm is basophilic because of dense rough ER. The apical cytoplasm is eosinophilic because of zymogen granules. They secrete trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, procarboxypeptidases, proelastase, amylase and lipase.
- **Centroacinar cells** are pale cells inside the acinus. They mark where the intercalated duct begins, and seeing them is diagnostic of pancreas rather than parotid. These cells and the intercalated duct cells secrete **bicarbonate**-rich fluid through CFTR, which drives Cl⁻/HCO₃⁻ exchange.
- The duct path runs intercalated, then intralobular, then interlobular, then the main duct (of Wirsung). The main duct joins the common bile duct at the ampulla. The **sphincter of Oddi** guards this opening.
- Unlike the parotid, the pancreas has no striated ducts and no myoepithelial cells.

**Control.** **Secretin**, released by duodenal S cells in response to acid, drives the bicarbonate output. **CCK**, released by I cells in response to fat and protein, along with vagal acetylcholine, drives enzyme release.

**Endocrine islets.** These are pale, richly capillarized cords.
- **β cells** (about 60-70%) make insulin and sit mostly centrally in rodents.
- **α cells** (about 15-20%) make glucagon.
- **δ cells** make somatostatin.
- **PP cells** make pancreatic polypeptide, and **ε cells** make ghrelin.

The capillaries are fenestrated.

**Gallbladder.** The layers are mucosa (tall columnar absorptive cells with microvilli, plus lamina propria), a loosely arranged muscularis externa, perimuscular connective tissue, and serosa or adventitia. There is no muscularis mucosae or submucosa. Mucosal glands appear only near the neck.

The epithelium uses Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase and paracellular water flow through lateral spaces, which often look dilated on slides. This concentrates bile roughly 5-10×. **Rokitansky-Aschoff sinuses** are deep outpouchings of mucosa into the muscle. They are associated with chronic inflammation and can trap bacteria and stones.
levels.phd:
**Acinar secretion** is the textbook secretory pathway. Palade's pulse-chase autoradiography in guinea-pig pancreas, using ³H-leucine, traced newly made protein from rough ER to Golgi to condensing vacuoles to zymogen granules to exocytosis. That work underpinned his 1974 Nobel Prize.

CCK and acetylcholine both act on Gq-coupled receptors to raise Ca²⁺. Acinar cells generate apical Ca²⁺ spikes that trigger granule fusion.

Whether human acinar cells express functional CCK1 receptors is debated. Evidence suggests that, in humans, CCK may act mainly through vagal afferent and cholinergic neural circuits.

**Autoprotection** works in several layers:
- Enzymes are stored as zymogens.
- Trypsinogen is activated only in the duodenal lumen, by brush-border enteropeptidase.
- **SPINK1** (pancreatic secretory trypsin inhibitor) is co-packaged with the zymogens.
- Trypsin can cleave and inactivate itself.

Premature intra-acinar trypsinogen activation, for example by cathepsin B after lysosome and zymogen co-localization, initiates pancreatitis. Gain-of-function **PRSS1** mutations (such as R122H) cause hereditary pancreatitis.

**Ductal HCO₃⁻ secretion** can reach about 140 mM. This relies on CFTR and SLC26A6 working at the apical membrane, with WNK/SPAK kinases shifting CFTR toward conducting HCO₃⁻. In cystic fibrosis, the low-volume, protein-rich juice plugs the ducts. The result is acinar atrophy and fibrosis, which is the 'cystic fibrosis of the pancreas' Andersen described in 1938.

**Islet architecture differs by species.** Rodent islets have a β-cell core and a non-β mantle. Human islets are intermingled, with many α cells directly beside β cells. This supports strong paracrine crosstalk:
- Insulin, zinc and GABA suppress α cells.
- δ-cell somatostatin restrains both α and β cells.

Islet blood flow direction is still debated, with models running core-to-mantle or along mixed routes.

**Gallbladder concentration** depends on apical NHE3 and Cl⁻/HCO₃⁻ exchange coupled to basolateral Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase. Water moves through aquaporins and lateral intercellular spaces. Bile salt concentration can rise many-fold while osmolality stays roughly isotonic, because bile salts form micelles that are osmotically inefficient.

Gallstones form through three linked defects: cholesterol supersaturation, nucleation, and **hypomotility**. Smooth-muscle CCK1-receptor dysfunction is one documented cause of reduced emptying.
levels.expert:
**Pancreatic pathology at the bench.** The duct-cell-versus-acinar-cell origin of **pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma** has been revised by lineage tracing. In mouse models, acinar cells carrying Kras^G12D undergo **acinar-to-ductal metaplasia (ADM)**. This shift, which inflammation strongly promotes, gives rise to PanIN precursors. Mutations then accumulate in a typical order: KRAS early, then CDKN2A, then TP53 and SMAD4.

In practice, distinguishing well-differentiated PDAC from reactive ducts in chronic pancreatitis is a classic diagnostic trap. Features favouring cancer include:
- perineural invasion
- glands lying next to muscular vessels
- incomplete lumens
- marked variation in nuclear size

SMAD4 loss on immunohistochemistry also supports malignancy.

**Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours** stain for chromogranin and synaptophysin. Their grade is set by Ki-67 index and mitotic count under the WHO system. Note that islets trapped within atrophic, fibrotic pancreas can aggregate into clusters that mimic a tumour.

**Islet frontiers** fall into three main areas.
- **Type 1 diabetes:** network studies of donor pancreas (nPOD) show insulitis is patchy and lobular. Some β cells persist for decades after diagnosis.
- **Type 2 diabetes:** β-cell dedifferentiation, rather than pure cell death, is proposed to contribute.
- **Therapy:** stem-cell-derived islet products (for example, Vertex's zimislecel, formerly VX-880) have restored insulin independence in some trial participants with type 1 diabetes. Immune protection and the site of implantation are still open problems.

**For a future surgeon.** The Whipple procedure (pancreaticoduodenectomy) depends on the frozen-section margin at the pancreatic neck and the bile duct. A postoperative pancreatic fistula is more likely with a soft, non-fibrotic gland that has a small duct, because intact, enzyme-rich acini leak through the anastomosis.

**Gallbladder.** Several conditions shape how gallbladder specimens are read.
- **Cholesterolosis:** foamy macrophages in the lamina propria give the 'strawberry gallbladder' appearance.
- **Adenomyomatosis:** exaggerated Rokitansky-Aschoff sinuses produce a 'comet-tail' artefact on ultrasound.
- **Porcelain gallbladder:** a calcified wall. The cancer risk is now judged lower than historical estimates, particularly for diffuse calcification.

Because the gallbladder lacks a submucosa, tumour that invades the muscle sits close to the liver and lymphatics. This explains why T staging matters so much. Incidental cancer found after cholecystectomy for stones usually prompts consideration of re-resection once the tumour has invaded into the muscle layer, conventionally T1b or deeper.

**Open questions** remain about how much human pancreatic acini depend on direct CCK signalling, and about how the human islet microcirculation is organised.

keyPoints: Pancreas is ~98% exocrine acini and ~1-2% endocrine islets
Acinar cells: basophilic basal rough ER, eosinophilic apical zymogen granules
Centroacinar cells and ducts secrete bicarbonate via CFTR, driven by secretin
Islets: beta cells make insulin, alpha glucagon, delta somatostatin
Enzymes are stored inactive; early trypsin activation causes pancreatitis
Gallbladder: columnar epithelium, no submucosa, concentrates bile; CCK triggers emptying

test.q: Why is the base of a pancreatic acinar cell basophilic?
test.explain: Ribosomal RNA on rough ER binds hematoxylin. The apex is pink because of its zymogen granules.

test.q: Which cells sit inside an acinus and are diagnostic of pancreas rather than parotid?
test.explain: Centroacinar cells are the start of the intercalated duct. The pancreas lacks myoepithelial cells and striated ducts.

test.q: Which hormone mainly stimulates bicarbonate-rich pancreatic fluid?
test.explain: Acid in the duodenum releases secretin from S cells. Secretin drives CFTR-dependent HCO₃⁻ secretion by ducts.

test.q: Which islet cell type is the most numerous?
test.explain: Beta cells make up roughly 60-70% of islet cells and secrete insulin.

test.q: Why are pancreatic enzymes stored as zymogens?
choices: To let them pass into the bloodstream
To speed their release into ducts
To make them stain more brightly
To keep them from digesting the gland
test.explain: Inactive precursors protect the pancreas. Premature activation leads to pancreatitis.

test.q: Which layer is missing from the gallbladder wall?
test.explain: The gallbladder has no submucosa and no muscularis mucosae, unlike the intestine.

test.q: What epithelium lines the gallbladder?
test.explain: Tall simple columnar absorptive cells line the gallbladder and concentrate bile.

test.q: Which hormone makes the gallbladder contract after a fatty meal?
choices: Secretin, from duodenal and jejunal S cells
Glucagon, from pancreatic islet alpha cells
Gastrin, from gastric antral G cells
test.explain: CCK, released by duodenal I cells, contracts the gallbladder and stimulates enzyme release.

test.q: Rokitansky-Aschoff sinuses are:
choices: Ducts that drain bile from the liver
Mucosal outpouchings into the muscle layer
Clusters of endocrine cells in the pancreas
test.explain: They are deep outpouchings of gallbladder mucosa into the muscle, associated with chronic inflammation.

test.q: Pale endocrine patches in the pancreas are called the islets of ___.
test.explain: They are named after Paul Langerhans, who described them in 1869.

test.q: What are the pink apical granules that store inactive digestive enzymes in acinar cells called?
test.explain: Zymogen granules hold inactive proenzymes until exocytosis.

test.q: Hard deposits that form when bile becomes supersaturated with cholesterol are called ___.
test.explain: Supersaturation, nucleation and poor emptying all contribute to gallstones.

kidTest.q: What does the gallbladder store?
kidTest.explain: The gallbladder stores bile, which helps break up fat.

kidTest.q: What do the pancreas islets make?
kidTest.explain: The islets make insulin, which helps your body use sugar.

kidTest.q: What do the acini of the pancreas make?
kidTest.explain: Acini make digestive juices that break food into tiny pieces.

kidTest.q: When does the gallbladder squeeze out bile?
kidTest.explain: Fatty food tells the gallbladder to squeeze bile into the gut.

kidTest.q: Bile helps break up this kind of food: f _ _
kidTest.explain: Bile breaks up fat, like soap breaking up grease.

advancedTest.q: A gain-of-function PRSS1 mutation causes hereditary pancreatitis mainly because:
choices: Trypsin resists its own inactivation in acini
Enteropeptidase is absent from the duodenal lumen
Beta cells release excess insulin into the ducts
advancedTest.explain: PRSS1 variants such as R122H resist trypsin's self-inactivation. Active trypsin then persists inside the acinus and drives autodigestion.

advancedTest.q: In cystic fibrosis, pancreatic damage arises chiefly because:
choices: Acinar cells fail to make any zymogens
CCK receptors are missing from smooth muscle
Low bicarbonate fluid lets protein plug the ducts
Islet beta cells are destroyed by autoimmunity
advancedTest.explain: Defective CFTR reduces ductal HCO₃⁻ and fluid. Protein-rich secretions then obstruct ducts, causing acinar atrophy and fibrosis.

advancedTest.q: Why can the gallbladder concentrate bile salts many-fold yet keep bile roughly isotonic?
choices: The epithelium is fully impermeable to water
Micelles pack many salts into few particles
Bile salts are pumped back out into the blood
Mucus binds and neutralizes most bile salts
advancedTest.explain: Bile salts aggregate into micelles, which are osmotically inefficient. Solute content rises while osmolality barely changes.

advancedTest.q: Which finding most favours pancreatic adenocarcinoma over reactive ducts in chronic pancreatitis?
advancedTest.explain: Perineural invasion supports malignancy. Fibrosis and aggregated islets occur in benign chronic pancreatitis and can mimic tumour.
